description: We are a group of students from the University of San Carlos of Guatemala, here to solve problems and bring people and ideas together.
summary:
OrbiCultivo is a website that helps farmers in Guatemala decide what to plant, using satellite data from NASA. The farmer marks their land on a map and says what they grow (corn, beans, coffee, cardamom, vegetables or sugarcane), what their soil is like and what they want to achieve. The site then checks NASA POWER, NASA's service for rainfall, temperature and soil moisture records, and shows a traffic light for three risks: lack of water, frost and moisture left around the roots. It can also simulate a dry year (El Niño) or a rainy one (La Niña).

It then compares three paths: planting the same crop again, rotating with plants that feed the soil, or switching to crops that withstand drought. Each piece of advice names the NASA mission behind it: SMAP for soil moisture, GPM for rainfall and ECOSTRESS for heat in plants, and reminds the farmer to check the soil by hand.
details:
What it does

OrbiCultivo is a web platform that turns NASA climate data into planting advice for small farmers in Guatemala. The farmer finds their land on a map, or searches among 54 municipalities, and tells us what they grow (corn, beans, coffee, cardamom, vegetables or sugarcane), what their soil is like and what they want to achieve.

With that, the platform pulls the last 60 days of daily data from NASA POWER for those coordinates: rainfall, minimum and maximum temperature, and root-zone soil moisture. It compares the rain against the water the crop needs and shows three plain-language indicators: water shortage, frost risk and moisture at the roots. The farmer can also simulate a dry El Niño year or a rainy La Niña year.

Finally, it compares three paths for the next season: repeating the same crop, rotating with cover legumes such as Canavalia or Mucuna that return nitrogen to the soil, or switching to drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers in the Dry Corridor and the highlands lose harvests to the mid-summer dry spell and to frost. We want them to see those risks before planting and to have a concrete alternative to monoculture, so they spend less on fertilizer and keep a harvest in bad years.

What makes it creative

Every recommendation comes with three things: the NASA mission whose science supports it (SMAP, GPM, ECOSTRESS or POWER), what the satellite cannot see at plot scale, and a check the farmer can do by hand, such as digging 20 cm to feel the moisture. A built-in guide explains the satellites and translates scientific terms into everyday farming words.

What we considered

  • Language: soil types are named the way farmers call them, and there is no jargon on screen.
  • Honesty about the data: satellite cells cover several kilometers, so the tool advises and the farmer decides.
  • Connectivity: if NASA POWER is unreachable, the platform falls back to regional reference values.
  • Local support: the advice points to extension agents and the national weather service.

Tools

  • Data: NASA POWER API; Copernicus Data Space for Sentinel-2 scenes and NDVI.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, and Recharts.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose.
  • License: open source under GPL-3.0.

Current state and next steps

Today only NASA POWER is queried live. SMAP, GPM and ECOSTRESS are cited as the scientific basis of each recommendation, and the yearly rainfall chart uses typical regional patterns. Next we plan to connect those missions directly, show Sentinel-2 vegetation data to the farmer, and rank the strategies by the farmer's stated goal.
